value.overview: The Ruddy-breasted Seedeater is a small seed-eating songbird of open tropical habitats. It belongs to the tanager family and is usually found in grasslands, savannas, marsh edges, scrub, and other lightly or heavily modified open areas. Males are more colorful, with grayish upperparts and rich cinnamon or rufous underparts, while females and immature birds are plainer brown. The species occurs from Mexico through Central America and across much of northern and central South America.
value.classification: The Ruddy-breasted Seedeater is a passerine in the tanager family, Thraupidae. Its scientific name is Sporophila minuta; several geographic subspecies are recognized.
value.identification: This is a very small, short-tailed finch-like bird with a stout conical bill. The adult male has gray to gray-brown upperparts, a darker head and face, rufous or cinnamon rump and underparts, and noticeable pale markings along the folded wings. Females and immature birds are warm buffy brown above and paler below, with less contrast and no strong rufous coloring. Its small size, thick bill, open-country habits, and cinnamon tones help separate it from other seedeaters.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from Mexico and Central America to Colombia, Venezuela, the Guianas, Brazil, Ecuador, and Trinidad and Tobago. In Costa Rica it is a resident, locally common bird rather than a widespread species of all regions. It is especially associated with the Térraba and Río Frío savannas and grasslands, and it also occurs in the Coto and Golfo Dulce lowlands. Typical habitats include grassy savannas, marshes, scrub, roadsides, gardens, and disturbed open areas.
value.migrationStatus: Generally resident in Costa Rica, with local movements after breeding and possible wider dispersal when birds form larger feeding flocks. Costa Rican records indicate year-round occurrence, especially in suitable lowland grasslands and savannas.
value.breeding: In Costa Rica, breeding has been recorded mainly from June through August, although reproductive activity may extend later in some years. The nest is a small open cup made from grass stems, rootlets, and other plant fibers. It is usually placed low, within a grass clump or dense low shrub, commonly below one meter but occasionally higher in a small tree. Two or three nestlings have been reported in Costa Rica; detailed information on eggs there remains limited.
value.dietFeeding: The Ruddy-breasted Seedeater feeds mainly on small grass and other herbaceous seeds, which it removes with its strong conical bill. It usually forages in seed-bearing grasses and weeds in open ground, marsh edges, and scrub. During the breeding season, adults may also take small insects or other invertebrates, particularly when additional protein is needed for developing young. It often feeds in pairs, small groups, or mixed flocks with other seedeaters.
value.behavior: This active, inconspicuous bird usually moves through grasses and low vegetation, often perching briefly on exposed stems or shrubs. Males sing from visible perches, especially during the breeding season, while females and immature birds are more subdued in appearance. Outside the breeding period, groups may become larger and travel farther in search of seed resources. The species is frequently encountered in open, human-altered landscapes as well as natural savannas and wetlands.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not clearly quantified, but the species is generally regarded as widespread and not undergoing a known rapid overall decline.
